name: Question 7
problem: Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of ${x}^{-1/2}$ about $x=9$ to approximate the value of ${8}^{-1/2}.$
worked_solution:
We use Taylor's formula in the form

$$
f(x)=f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{{f}^{″}(a)}{2!}(x-a)^{2}+⋯,
$$

with $a=9.$ 

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ={x}^{-1/2} \\ f(9) & ={9}^{-1/2}=\frac{1}{3} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{-3/2} \\ {f}^{′}(9) & =-\frac{1}{2}(9)^{-3/2}=-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the Taylor series is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-1/2} & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{2\cdot 27}(x-9)+⋯ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-\frac{x-9}{54}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute $x=8$ into the above to approximate ${8}^{-1/2}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{8}^{-1/2} & ≈\frac{1}{3}-\frac{8-9}{54} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{54} \\  & =\frac{19}{54}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Use the first two non-zero terms of the Taylor expansion of x−1/2 about x=9 to approximate the value of 8−1/2.

a
8−1/2≈1781
b
8−1/2≈827
c
8−1/2≈512
d
8−1/2≈34
e
8−1/2≈1954
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We use Taylor's formula in the form f(x)=f(a)+f′(a)(x−a)+f″(a)2!(x−a)2+⋯, with a=9.

Calculating the necessary derivatives, we get

f(x)=x−1/2f(9)=9−1/2=13f′(x)=−12x−3/2f′(9)=−12(9)−3/2=−12⋅27.

So, the Taylor series is x−1/2=13−12⋅27(x−9)+⋯=13−x−954+⋯.

We substitute x=8 into the above to approximate 8−1/2. We get

8−1/2≈13−8−954=13+154=1954.
